97 CASE REPORTS Survival After Bilateral Adrenal Hemorrhage During Heparin Therapy JOHN KLASSEN, M.D.* and BEVERLY E. P. MURPHY, M. D, Ph.D., f Montreal "DECAUSE it is a condition which continues.*-* to be associated with a high mortality rate, despite the fact that treatment is available for it, spontaneous adrenal hemorrhage deserves greater clinical attention. Many factors are said to predispose to such hemorrhage, including septicemia, pregnancy, hemorrhagic diseases, trauma, leukemia, lymphoma and other neo¬ plasia.30, 31 Anticoagulant therapy has been con¬ sidered causative in some 35 patients described in the literature, only three of whom survived.1"4 Both heparin and coumarin compounds have been implicated.

The present case report de¬ scribes a patient receiving heparin therapy who survived bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. It illus¬ trates some of the difficulties of making an early diagnosis in this condition. The pathophysiology of this disorder is briefly reviewed.

A 74year-old veteran first presented at the Queen Mary Veterans Hospital in 1949 with a possible myocardial infarction. He was hospitalized in 1951 for mild heart failure which responded to digitaliza¬ tion. On January 14, 1966, he was admitted again because of moderate dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, intermittent paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and se¬ vere cough especially when prone, for many years.

He sought medical advice because of the increasing severity of his symptoms. He had smoked two packages of cigarettes daily until 1944 but none since. His sputum had recently become purulent and amounted to one cup per day.
No fever or chills had been noted. It could not be determined defin¬ itely whether he had angina pectoris. Shortly before admission he had pain in his right calf.

Intermittent ankle edema and bilateral varicose veins had been present for many years. There was no history of exposure to tuberculosis. On examination, he was afebrile and had an ir¬ regular heart rate of 156 per minute, a blood pre- ?

No excessive pigmentation was noted. A radiograph of the chest was negative and the elec¬ trocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response. The patient was digitalized, intermittent positivepressure breathing was started and, because of a moderate growth of pneumococci from his sputum, he was given penicillin.

On this regimen his symptomatic and clinical improvement was marked. On January 18, signs of a superficial thrombo¬ phlebitis appeared in the right calf. He was treated with bed rest, hot foments, and elevation of the leg.

In addition, heparin 50 to 75 mg. was admin¬ istered intravenously every six hours to keep the clotting time four hours after the injection at 25 to 30 minutes (control: 7 minutes). Despite these measures, over the next five to six days the inflam¬ mation spread up to the saphenofemoral junction. Repeated urinalyses were negative, and many stools were also negative for occult blood.

Marked abdominal distension, vomit¬ ing and absent bowel sounds developed. A plain film of the abdomen showed dilated loops of small bowel, and the psoas shadows could not be definitely identified. His hemoglobin, which was 15.7 g. per 100 ml. on admission, had fallen to 11.2 per 100 ml.
On January 31 and further to 9.4 per 100 ml. On February 4. The platelet count varied from 170,000 to 300,000, and at no time was there any evidence of a generalized bleeding diathesis.

An initial and only dose of phenprocoumon (Marcumar) 18 mg. was given on February 1 and the patient's pro¬ thrombin time on February 3 was 30 sec. (control 14 sec). At this time, he was believed to be suffer¬ ing from retroperitoneal hemorrhage and the heparin was stopped.

The symptoms and signs gradually subsided over the next three days, by which time the thrombophlebitis was also clearing. On February 2 a major motor seizure occurred which was without localizing signs and left no residual neurological deficit. When this value was reported on February 20, adrenal insufficiency was considered likely and a fourhour intravenous adrenocorticotropic (ACTH) test was performed on February 21.

Plasma cortisol determinations were made at 0, 2, 4 and 6 hours after starting a fourhour intravenous infusion of 75 units adrenocorticotropin (Acton X) in 40 ml. 5% glucose in water.5 A low initial plasma cortisol level of 2.5 fig. Per 100 ml. Rising to a maximum at four hours of only 5.4 fig.

Per 100 ml. was reported the same day, and oral cortisone 37.5 mg . Daily was begun after sev¬ eral intramuscular injections of cortisol hemisuccinate (Solucortef) had been given. This replacement therapy produced definite clinical improvement.

Per litre to 2225 mEq. Per litre. Since he seemed to have slight residual adrenocortical func¬ tion, his response to ACTH stimulation was assessed again on March 18 and on April 21 to 25 to deter¬ mine if any regeneration of adrenal tissue might have occurred.

During these periods his steroid therapy was changed to dexamethasone 0.75 mg. daily because this drug is not measured in the assay. Since, by April 21, he had been receiving cortisone for two months, the intravenous test was done after the intramuscular administration of 120 units of ACTH daily for three days. On both these occasions the initial plasma cortisol levels were neg¬ ligible, and they did not rise during ACTH adminis¬ tration.

In April, repeat renal function tests were within normal limits. At time of writing the patient feels very well, has no specific complaints, and walks long distances daily. His dyspnea and cough have disappeared.
His current medications include digitalis, cortisone ace¬ tate 37.5 mg. per day, and 9afluorohydrocortisone 0.1 mg. per day. On exposure to the sun he has developed a good tan. Discussion

The clinical course of patients who develop adrenal hemorrhage while on anticoagulants is not so characteristic as the fulminant course of the WaterhouseFriderichsen syndrome where shock, hyperpyrexia, extensive purpura and hy¬ poglycemia usually occur within 24 hours. The latter condition occurs mainly in children and young adults while the former is more common in persons 50 to 70 years of age and is generally associated with severe illness such as myocardial infarction or pulmonary embolism. According to Amador,1 who recently re¬ viewed the clinical features of 30 such cases, the hemorrhage occurred 2 to 13 days after antico¬ agulant therapy was begun, and there was no evidence of generalized bleeding. Contrary to the general view expressed by Cahill, Jenkins and Thorn,6 excessive anticoagulant therapy did not appear to be responsible. Severe crampy upper abdominal pain with tenderness and guarding occurred most commonly, often ac¬ companied by nausea and vomiting.

Death occurred in two to eight days. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage was infrequent, mimicking an acute "surgical" abdomen. In most patients the adrenal hemorrhage was bilateral, but a few have been reported with unilateral hemorrhage who sur¬ vived following operation.79 Close analysis of cases of adrenal hemorrhage suggests that clin¬ ical acumen and perspicacity is necessary if these cases are to be diagnosed during life.10, n

In this diagnosis, Amador believes that an eosinophil count above 50 per c.mm. is a most useful, although not specific, test. Certainly in the acute situation the collection and processing of 24 hour urine samples for 17ketosteroids, 17hydroxysterdids and/or 17ketogenic steroids is much too slow. The determination of corticoids in random plasma samples is helpful but not fully adequate, since many factors can affect the plasma level.

Indeed, the only satisfactory way of proving adrenal insufficiency is to demon¬ strate the inability to respond to ACTH. With newer methods of measuring steroids in plasma, a definitive diagnosis can be made within a few hours. Two rapid procedures for steroid determi¬ nations are available: fluorescence analysis and competitive proteinbinding analysis.

Their rela¬ tive merits have been discussed recently.12 In the case under discussion, once the possibility of adrenal insufficiency was seriously considered, the diagnosis was confirmed the next day using the competitive proteinbinding method. In a seriously ill patient, dexamethasone and/or 9afluorohydrocortisone can be given during the these ACTH test, not measured by this procedure.

When such tests are not available immediately, the safest course is to treat the patient with steroids after first taking a blood specimen that is sent away for analysis at once. The diagnosis should be con¬ firmed later by an ACTH test. If there is no adrenal insufficiency, no harm will have been done by the administration of high doses of steroids if these are not continued for more than two or three days.

Pretreatment of the animals with heparin did not prevent the adrenal hemorrhage. Elaboration of adrenergic vasoactive substances by the adrenals did not seem to play a significant role in the pathogenesis.
